rubric.note: Practice rubric only; not official MAWA admissions scoring.

items.title: The reverse-number detective
items.prompt:
A three-digit number ABC means 100A+10B+C. Reverse its digits, then subtract the smaller number from the larger. Show reversed numbers and differences with three digit places, including a leading zero if needed.

a) Find the difference for 741, 502 and 811.
b) Try three other starting numbers whose first and last digits differ. What do you notice about the middle digit of each three-digit answer?
c) Show why the middle digit must always be 9. What happens if the first and last starting digits are equal?
items.hint: Compare what changes and what stays the same when only the middle starting digit changes.
items.trap: Examples are evidence, not proof for every number.
items.solution: 741−147=594; 502−205=297; 811−118=693. In general, (100A+10B+C)−(100C+10B+A)=99(A−C). The positive difference is 99d for d=1,…,9: 099,198,…,891, so the middle digit is 9. If A=C, the difference is 000.

items.title: Odd tiles become cubes
items.prompt:
A square grows by adding the next odd-number strip. Another puzzle is to make cubes by adding consecutive odd numbers.

a) Find 1+3+5+…+31 without adding all sixteen terms.
b) Explain why 13+15+17+19 is a perfect cube. Find five consecutive odd numbers whose sum is 125.
c) For positive n, explain why the n consecutive odd numbers centred on n² total n³.
items.hint: Draw square dots for 1,4,9,16 and identify the new strip each time.
items.trap: The nth odd number is not the same as the sum of the first n odd numbers.
items.solution: The first sixteen odd numbers sum to 16²=256. 13+15+17+19=64=4³. Five odd numbers centred on 25 are 21,23,25,27,29 and total 125. In general n consecutive odd numbers centred on n² have average n² and there are n terms, so total n³.

items.title: Three lanterns, one flash
items.prompt:
Three lanterns flash at time 0. Red flashes every 4 seconds, blue every 6 seconds and green every 9 seconds.

a) At what first positive time do all three flash together?
b) At 12 seconds, which flash?
c) Replace green by an 8-second lantern. How does (a) change, and why is your time the first?
items.hint: List multiples, then use the least common multiple idea.
items.trap: Multiplying all periods gives a common time but not necessarily the first.
items.solution: LCM(4,6,9)=36. At 12 seconds red and blue flash, not green. LCM(4,6,8)=24; it is the first because any simultaneous flash must be a common multiple and 24 is the least.

items.title: Five badges in a line
items.prompt:
Five different badges A,B,C,D,E are arranged in a line. C is not at either end. A and B are not adjacent.

a) How many arrangements satisfy both rules?
b) Give a systematic method proving no valid arrangement was missed or repeated.
c) Give one valid and one invalid arrangement and identify the broken rule.
items.hint: Count arrangements with C interior, then subtract those with A and B adjacent.
items.trap: Do not merge AB and BA; they are different orders.
items.solution: With C in one of three interior positions there are 3×4!=72 arrangements. For each C position, exactly 8 have A and B adjacent, so 24 invalid. Valid=72−24=48.

items.title: Two rows of dots
items.prompt:
There are five dots on one straight line and four on a parallel lower line. A triangle uses any three dots not all on the same line.

a) How many triangles can be made?
b) Explain why every real triangle is counted exactly once.
c) Generalise to m upper dots and n lower dots.
items.hint: Count two-top-one-bottom OR two-bottom-one-top.
items.trap: Three collinear dots do not form a triangle.

items.title: Paths around the blocked gate
items.prompt:
An explorer goes from S=(0,0) to T=(4,3) using only one-square Right or Up moves. F=(2,1) is blocked.

a) How many shortest paths exist without the block?
b) How many shortest paths pass through F, and how many avoid it?
c) Explain why multiplying routes to F by routes from F is legitimate; give an alternative check.
items.hint: Represent a shortest path as seven R/U symbols.
items.trap: Do not count longer detours when the problem asks for shortest paths.
items.solution: All shortest paths: C(7,3)=35. To F: C(3,1)=3; F to T: C(4,2)=6; through F=18; avoid F=17. The product rule works because each pair of segments gives one unique path through F.

items.title: Triangles in a fan
items.prompt:
Five rays leave a point A and meet a baseline. Two more horizontal lines cross all five rays, parallel to the baseline.

a) Count all triangles in the drawing.
b) Explain why every triangle contains A and cannot have two horizontal sides.
c) Generalise to r rays and h horizontal levels including the baseline.
items.hint: For one horizontal level, choose a pair of rays.
items.trap: Non-neighbouring rays also create larger triangles.
items.solution: Choose two of 5 rays and one of 3 horizontal levels: C(5,2)×3=30. General formula h·r(r−1)/2.

items.title: The round-ended window
items.prompt:
A window consists of a rectangle 8r long and 2r high plus one semicircle of radius r outside each short side.

a) Find total height and width.
b) Find exact area and perimeter.
c) The smallest enclosing rectangle is 10r by 2r. Find the area inside it but outside the window.
items.hint: The two semicircles make one whole circle.
items.trap: Area and perimeter have different units and scale differently.
items.solution: Height=2r, width=10r. Area=(16+π)r². Perimeter=(16+2π)r. Uncovered area=(4−π)r².

items.title: The missing quarter-circle
items.prompt:
A square has side 4r. A quarter-circle of radius 2r centred at the top-right corner is cut away.

a) Find exact remaining area.
b) Find exact perimeter including the curved edge.
c) Explain why area and perimeter formulas cannot be interchanged.
items.hint: Trace the outside boundary after the cut.
items.trap: The new curved edge must be added to the remaining straight boundary.
items.solution: Remaining area=(16−π)r². Straight boundary left=12r; quarter-circle arc=πr; perimeter=(12+π)r.

items.title: Four slides to the corners
items.prompt:
On a 3×3 board, four discs start at the middle squares of the four edges. A move slides one disc one square horizontally or vertically into an empty square. The goal is one disc in each corner.

a) Give a four-move solution.
b) Prove fewer than four moves is impossible.
c) Explain the difference between a construction and a proof of minimality.
items.hint: Count how many discs start on squares forbidden in the final position.
items.trap: A four-move construction alone does not prove optimality.
items.solution: Move each edge-middle disc once to a neighbouring corner. At least four moves are necessary because all four discs start off-corner and every disc must move at least once. Construction+lower bound proves minimum 4.

items.title: The five painted faces
items.prompt:
A 3×4×5 block is made of unit cubes. The top and four vertical sides are painted; the bottom is not.

a) How many small cubes have paint on at least one face?
b) How many have exactly three painted faces?
c) How many have exactly two painted faces? Avoid double-counting.
items.hint: Count unpainted cubes first; then separate top-edge and vertical-edge cases.
items.trap: The bottom is not painted.
items.solution: Total 60. Unpainted=(3−1)(4−2)(5−2)=12, so painted=48. Exactly three painted faces: 4 top corners. Exactly two: 10 top-edge non-corners +8 vertical-edge cubes below top=18.

items.title: Two corners of a chessboard
items.prompt:
Colour a 4×4 board like a chessboard. A domino covers two edge-adjacent squares.

a) Remove top-left and bottom-right. Can seven dominoes tile the rest? Prove it.
b) Instead remove top-left and bottom-left. Can seven dominoes tile the rest? Give a construction.
c) Explain why even area is not sufficient for tileability.
items.hint: Count the two colours after removing the squares.
items.trap: A failed drawing is not an impossibility proof.
items.solution: In (a) the removed corners have the same colour, leaving a 6/8 colour imbalance; seven dominoes would need 7 of each, impossible. In (b) a tiling exists: one vertical domino in the two remaining cells of column 1 and two vertical dominoes in each of columns 2–4.

items.title: Unlock the three-symbol code
items.prompt:
Different digits A,B,C are chosen from 1,2,3,4,5 with A+B=7 and B+C=5.

a) List all assignments satisfying these two clues.
b) Add 2A+C=10. Which remains?
c) Explain why the first two clues are insufficient but the third gives uniqueness.
items.hint: Choose B first, then A=7−B and C=5−B.
items.trap: Every clue must be checked, not just one equation.
items.solution: Candidates are (3,4,1),(4,3,2),(5,2,3). Only (4,3,2) satisfies 2A+C=10.

items.title: Nine numbers, one magic square
items.prompt:
Place digits 1–9 once in a 3×3 square so every row, column and both long diagonals have the same total.

a) What must each line total?
b) Give a working square and check all eight lines.
c) Prove the centre must be 5 in every such square.
items.hint: Add 1+2+…+9 before placing any digit.
items.trap: Checking rows alone is not enough.
items.solution: Digits total 45, so each row totals 15. Example 8 1 6 / 3 5 7 / 4 9 2. Adding middle row, middle column and two diagonals gives 60; outside digits count once, centre four times: 60=45+3c, so c=5.

items.title: Six coins, two secret payments
items.prompt:
You have exactly six coins, each worth 1,2 or5 units.

a) Find all collections worth exactly 14.
b) Prove there are no others.
c) With exactly five coins of these denominations, can you make 24? Prove it.
items.hint: Start with the number of 5-unit coins.
items.trap: Different orders of the same coin counts are not different collections.
items.solution: Let counts x,y,z satisfy x+y+z=6 and x+2y+5z=14, giving y+4z=8. z=1 gives (x,y,z)=(1,4,1); z=2 gives (4,0,2). For five coins, max is 25; replacing any 5 by a 2 drops to at most22, so 24 is impossible.

items.title: Five islands and their bridges
items.prompt:
Five islands A–E require degrees 3,2,2,1,2 respectively; at most one bridge joins any pair.

a) Draw a network meeting the requirements.
b) How many bridges are required? Explain the double-count.
c) If E needed degree 3 instead of2, prove no arrangement is possible.
items.hint: Start by connecting the island needing three bridges.
items.trap: The degree sum counts each bridge twice.
items.solution: One construction: AB,AC,AD,BE,CE. Degree sum=10, so 5 bridges. If E had degree3, sum degrees=11, impossible because every ordinary graph has even total degree.

items.title: Four queens, no attacks
items.prompt:
A queen attacks along row, column and diagonals.

a) Place four non-attacking queens on a 4×4 board.
b) Why are five impossible on 4×4?
c) Can three non-attacking queens fit on 3×3? Give a complete argument.
items.hint: For 3×3, a three-queen solution would use every row and every column exactly once.
items.trap: One failed layout is not proof all layouts fail.
items.solution: Example 4×4 columns by rows: [2,4,1,3]. Five queens force two into one of four rows. On 3×3, any three queens correspond to one of 3!=6 column permutations; each has a diagonal attack, so at most two.

items.title: The best rectangle from a fence
items.prompt:
You have 24 one-metre fence sections and must make a rectangle with positive whole-number side lengths, using all sections.

a) List all rectangles ignoring rotations.
b) Which maximises area?
c) Prove no allowed rectangle has larger area.
items.hint: Turn perimeter 24 into a+b=12.
items.trap: Equal perimeter does not mean equal area.

items.title: The last stone wins
items.prompt:
A pile has 17 stones. Players alternate removing 1 or2; whoever takes the last stone wins.

a) Can the first player force a win? Give the opening.
b) Give a response rule that works against either opponent move.
c) If the pile begins with18, who can force a win?
items.hint: Test small piles and identify bad starting sizes.
items.trap: A strategy must work against both opponent responses.
items.solution: From17 remove2, leaving15. Then complement the opponent to remove3 per pair (1↔2), returning to smaller multiples of3 until zero. From18 the second player uses this strategy.

items.title: The old-money time traveller
items.prompt:
Old money used 1 pound=20 shillings and 1 shilling=12 pence.

a) Find £2/14/9 + £1/8/7.
b) Check by converting both amounts to pence.
c) Explain why decimal carrying would be wrong.
items.hint: Use separate pound, shilling and pence columns; start with pence.
items.trap: The carrying bases are 12 and20, not10 and10.
items.solution: 9+7=16 pence → carry1 shilling, leave4. 14+8+1=23 shillings → carry1 pound, leave3. Pounds=4, so £4/3/4. Pence check:657+343=1000; £4/3/4=1000.
